hints: Add the charge on the central metal ion to the total charge from all six identical negative ligands to find the overall charge.
walkthrough:
Add up charges to get the overall charge**
Think of a complex formula as a simple sum. For A you have one $\text{Fe}^{3+}$ plus six $\text{CN}^{-}$ ions. That is $(+3) + 6(-1) = -3$. So the ion is written with square brackets around the whole unit as $\text{[Fe(CN)}_6\text{]}^{3-}$. For B you have one $\text{Fe}^{2+}$ plus six $\text{CN}^{-}$ ions. That is $(+2) + 6(-1) = -4$, giving $\text{[Fe(CN)}_6\text{]}^{4-}$.

Final answer: complex ion A: $\text{[Fe(CN)}_6\text{]}^{3-}$
complex ion B: $\text{[Fe(CN)}_6\text{]}^{4-}$

hints: Recall where colour in transition metal complexes comes from, splitting of the 3d orbitals into two sets and promotion of an electron between them by visible light.
Compare the central ions, $\text{Fe}^{3+}$ is $3\text{d}^5$ and $\text{Fe}^{2+}$ is $3\text{d}^6$, and think how different charge and electron configuration change the size of the splitting.
walkthrough:
Remember why complexes are coloured**
Picture the five 3d orbitals on iron. When six $\text{CN}^{-}$ ligands approach, the d-orbitals split into a lower set and a higher set separated by an energy gap called $\Delta E$. An electron can jump from the lower set to the upper set by absorbing exactly $\Delta E$ of energy from visible light. The colour you see is the light left over, the complementary colour to what was absorbed.

See why Fe(III) and Fe(II) give different gaps**
Here the ligand is the same, $\text{CN}^{-}$, but the metal is different. $\text{Fe}^{3+}$ has a higher charge and a $3\text{d}^5$ configuration, while $\text{Fe}^{2+}$ has a lower charge and a $3\text{d}^6$ configuration. The different nuclear charge pulling on the ligands and the different d-electron arrangement change how much the orbitals are split, so $\Delta E$ is different for A and B.

Link different gap to different colour**
Because $\Delta E = h\nu$, a different $\Delta E$ means a different frequency $\nu$ and wavelength of light is absorbed. If A absorbs one part of the visible spectrum and B absorbs another part, the transmitted light that reaches your eye is different, so the solutions appear different colours.

Final answer: The two complexes have different values of $\Delta E$, the energy gap between the split d-orbitals.
They therefore absorb light of different frequency / wavelength in the visible region, so different colours are transmitted / observed.

hints: Think about where the lone pair that forms the metal to ligand bond comes from, the ligand or shared equally.
walkthrough:
Spot who supplies the electrons**
A ligand like $\text{CN}^{-}$ has a lone pair on carbon. When it bonds to $\text{Fe}^{3+}$, that lone pair is donated into a vacant orbital on the iron. Because both shared electrons come from one atom, the ligand, this is the classic dative covalent bond, also called a coordinate bond.

hints: Use the number of ligands to predict the shape, six ligands points to octahedral, two ligands points to linear, and four ligands can be tetrahedral or square planar as stated.
Recall the standard bond angle for an octahedral complex with six identical positions and how to show 3D depth with wedges.
Contrast the two four coordinate cases, tetrahedral needs wedged bonds and $109.5^{\circ}$ while square planar is flat with $90^{\circ}$.
Remember to write the correct ligand formula around each metal and label one angle on every diagram, $180^{\circ}$ for the linear $\text{Ag}$ complex.
walkthrough:
Draw the octahedral Fe complex**
Six monodentate $\text{CN}^{-}$ ligands around $\text{Fe}$ always spread out as far as possible to give an octahedron. Put $\text{Fe}$ in the centre, draw four $\text{Fe}-\text{C}$ bonds in a plane with one wedge coming out and one hashed bond going back for the axial pair, then add the other two axial $\text{CN}$ ligands. Label any adjacent $\text{C}-\text{Fe}-\text{C}$ angle as $90^{\circ}$.

Draw the linear Ag complex**
Silver(I) with two $\text{NH}_3$ ligands has coordination number 2, so the ligands sit opposite each other to minimise repulsion. Draw $\text{H}_3\text{N}-\text{Ag}-\text{NH}_3$ as a straight line with $\text{Ag}$ in the middle. Label the $\text{N}-\text{Ag}-\text{N}$ angle as $180^{\circ}$. The formula is $\text{[Ag(NH}_3\text{)}_2\text{]}^{+}$.

Draw the tetrahedral Ni complex**
Nickel(0) with four $\text{CO}$ ligands bonded through C has coordination number 4 in a tetrahedral arrangement. Draw Ni in the centre with four $\text{Ni}-\text{C}$ bonds, using a solid wedge for one bond coming forward and a hashed wedge for one bond going back to show depth. Label any $\text{C}-\text{Ni}-\text{C}$ angle as $109.5^{\circ}$. The formula is $\text{[Ni(CO)}_4\text{]}$.

Draw the square planar Pd complex**
$\text{Pd}^{2+}$ with four $\text{Cl}^{-}$ ligands is specifically square planar, flat with all five atoms in one plane. Draw Pd in the centre with four $\text{Pd}-\text{Cl}$ bonds at right angles in a cross shape, no wedges needed because it is planar. Label any adjacent $\text{Cl}-\text{Pd}-\text{Cl}$ angle as $90^{\circ}$. The formula is $\text{[PdCl}_4\text{]}^{2-}$.

Final answer: complex ion A: octahedral $\text{Fe}$ with six $\text{CN}$ ligands, $90^{\circ}$ labelled.
$\text{Ag}^{+}$ with ammonia: linear $\text{H}_3\text{N}-\text{Ag}-\text{NH}_3$, $180^{\circ}$ labelled.
Ni with carbon monoxide: tetrahedral Ni with four $\text{CO}$ ligands bonded via C, $109.5^{\circ}$ labelled.
$\text{Pd}^{2+}$ with chloride: square planar Pd with four $\text{Cl}$ ligands, $90^{\circ}$ labelled.
All structures use wedge / hashed bonds where needed to show 3D shape.
